# `sort` — specification

Purpose, API and use: [README.md](README.md).

## Maturity

**Grade:** 2 · S1 E1 A2 H1 P2 · limited by audit (src changed since), performance (within 1.1× of the reference, not at it) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

**Scope:** ahead — Rust std `core::slice::sort` 1.93.1 (surveyed 2026-10-25): its three sorts with the same algorithms, plus the lead below

**Ahead:** feature — a stable sort without an allocator: `stableBuffer` sorts on caller scratch and `stable` returns `error.OutOfMemory`; Rust's `slice::sort` lives in `alloc`, aborts the process when the allocation fails and does not exist at all under `no_std` without an allocator (tests "stable matches std.sort.block exactly" `.min_buffer`, "stable reports OutOfMemory") (measured 2026-10-25)

**Audit:** review 2026-10-25 · mutation 2026-10-25 (124/198, 74 eq) · src 0e5dd8555967b7c5

**Hardening:** fuzz 2026-10-25 (8×200 000 seeds, reach 100 %) · ct n/a — sorts caller data by a caller comparator; no secret is held, and the comparison sequence depends on the data by design

**Performance:** ref 0.55–1.05× Rust std 1.93.1 · fastest 1.80× C++ libstdc++ 15 std::stable_sort (s_u64_saw: ascending runs of 1 000; also u_u64_tail 1.53× std::sort and sel_u64_asc 1.43× std::nth_element — nearly sorted input, where Rust is as slow; every other row ≤ 1.05× the faster of Rust std and libstdc++; JCC-mitigated builds on all sides, `tools/README.md`) (measured 2026-10-25)

**Evidence:** model-fuzz — `std.sort.block` (independent stable merge sort) as the model: key for key for `unstable`, byte for byte for `stable`, the k-th key and both sides for `selectNth`; inputs and scratch against guard pages; lying comparators checked for a permutation

**Known defects:** none recorded

**Downstream consumer:** no

**Where we are ahead:** a stable sort without an allocator (vs Rust std);
2–4× std's sorts; a lying comparator gets a permutation back instead of a
panic. **Where we are behind:** no radix or parallel sort (both separate
crates in Rust), no `partial_sort` (C++; `selectNth` + `unstable` on the
prefix does it), C++'s introsort is faster on nearly sorted input with a
random tail (as it is against Rust).

## What this module is, and what it is not

The three slice sorts of Rust's `core::slice::sort` (1.93.1), ported line by
line in structure: ipnsort (`unstable`), driftsort (`stable`,
`stableBuffer`) and introselect (`selectNth`), plus `asc`/`desc`/`bytesLess`
comparators. Given the same input and an honest comparator, each takes the
same decisions as Rust. The comparisons are Rust's too, with one exception:
for elements of 16 bytes or less, the pre-sorted-run check tests four
neighbours per branch and repeats up to four comparisons when a block leaves
the run. Counted on 100 000 random `u64` and 100 000 random 4–24-byte strings
(Rust / ours): unstable `u64` 1 722 052 / 1 722 055, stable `u64`
1 744 472 / 1 744 905, unstable strings 1 707 547 / 1 707 549.

Not here, and why:

- **No index-based `sortContext(a, b, ctx)` (std's `pdqContext` shape).**
  Both sorts move elements through a hole (a saved value and copies), not
  through `swap(i, j)`. A swap-only interface would need a different
  algorithm. Deferred; std's `pdqContext` covers it.
- **No radix sort.** Rust std has none. A radix path for integer keys is
  where a lead over Rust would come from. Deferred (Backlog).
- **No parallel sort.** Rust's rayon `par_sort` is a separate crate.
  Deferred.
- **No `sort_by_cached_key`.** In Zig it is a caller-side two-liner
  (compute the keys into an array, sort indices by them).

## Algorithm

Upstream design documents, by section:
[ipnsort](https://github.com/Voultapher/sort-research-rs/blob/main/writeup/ipnsort_introduction/text.md),
[driftsort](https://github.com/Voultapher/sort-research-rs/blob/main/writeup/driftsort_introduction/text.md),
[lomcyc partition](https://github.com/Voultapher/sort-research-rs/blob/main/writeup/lomcyc_partition/text.md).
The constants are Rust's, unchanged, and every one is named in the source:

| constant | value | where |
|---|---|---|
| always-insertion cut | 20 | `unstable.zig`, `stable.zig` |
| small-sort thresholds | 32 (network, ≤ 8-byte types; general, ≤ 85-byte types); 16 (fallback insertion) | `smallsort.zig` |
| branchless Lomuto partition | `@sizeOf(T) ≤ 96`; Hoare above | `unstable.zig` |
| quicksort budget | `2·⌊log2 n⌋` imbalanced partitions, then heapsort (unstable) or eager driftsort (stable) | |
| pseudo-median recursion | above 64 elements | `choosePivot` |
| stable scratch | `max(n − n/2, min(n, 8 MB / size), 48)`, on the stack when ≤ 4 KiB | `stable.zig` |
| run threshold | `min(64, n − n/2)` up to n = 4096, else ~√n | `drift` |
| introselect | 16 rounds, then median of ninthers; insertion ≤ 16 | `select.zig` |

What differs from Rust, deliberately:

1. **No panics on a broken order.** Rust's `bidirectional_merge` panics when
   its cursors do not meet. Here it returns `false`, and the caller restores
   a whole copy (`sort8Stable`, `smallSortGeneralWithScratch`) or keeps the
   unmerged halves (`smallSortNetwork`). The input stays a permutation either
   way. Rust's drop guards (`GapGuard`, `CopyOnDrop`, `MergeState`) exist only
   for unwinding out of a panicking comparator, which Zig cannot do. They
   became plain end-of-loop copies.
2. **The unstable partition copies the pivot into a local.** Rust keeps a
   reference, to observe interior mutability. A Zig element has none, and the
   copy lets the loop keep the pivot in registers.
3. **`noalias` on the pointer pairs that never overlap** (slice and scratch,
   merge source and destination). Rust gets that from `&mut`. Without it the
   stable partition reloaded the pivot on every element and did not
   vectorize the reversing copy-back: 1.40 G vs Rust's 0.79 G L1 loads on
   300 sorts of 100 000 `u64`, 1.08× the cycles. Now 1.02×.
4. **`stableBuffer` panics on scratch that is too short or overlaps the
   items.** The caller's mistake is not undefined behaviour.
5. **The run check of small elements goes four at a time** (`scanRun`).
   Rust's loop compiles to one load per element with the previous element
   kept in a register; ours, element by element, reloaded both neighbours
   (1.16× Rust on an ascending input). Carrying the previous element in a
   local did not help (two branches per element). Four comparisons and-ed
   per branch did: 0.98×.
6. **The stable partition copies back with loops, not `@memcpy`.** Without
   libc `@memcpy` is compiler_rt's `memcpy`, an out-of-line call that took
   13 % of a stable sort of 16 distinct keys; Rust's lands in glibc's AVX
   `memcpy`. The reversed right half goes back eight elements at a time
   through a fixed-size block, which LLVM turns into
   lane shuffles; the same loop written element by element stayed scalar
   whichever way it was indexed. Together: stable `u64` 1.10× → 1.03× Rust.
   Both only for elements of 16 bytes or less: for a 32-byte record they
   measured slower (stable `rec` 0.98× → 1.19×), and it keeps `@memcpy`.

## Memory safety under any comparator

Every index in the port is derived the way Rust's is, so whatever
`lessThan` answers, reads and writes stay in `items` and the scratch. The
sorts index through `[*]T`, which no build mode bounds-checks, so this is a
claim the tests have to check from outside:

- `fuzz_test.zig` places the items (and the caller's scratch) directly
  against a `PROT_NONE` page, at its tail or its head (`testkit.guard`). An
  access one element out of range faults under the seed that made it. A
  share of the runs use a comparator whose every answer is drawn from the
  fuzz source.
- `test_sort.zig` "lying comparator" tests: every element size, every
  entry point. They check for a permutation and for at most
  `64·(n+1)·(log2 n + 1)` comparisons.

## Limits and refusals

- `selectNth` panics on `index >= items.len` (Rust panics too).
- `stableBuffer` panics on `scratch.len < stableScratchLen(items.len)` or
  overlapping storage.
- `stable` returns `error.OutOfMemory` with `items` untouched (the scratch
  is allocated before anything moves; test "stable reports OutOfMemory").
- Zero-sized `T`: every entry point returns at once.

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class C · oracle n/a

There is no outside truth to agree with beyond "sorted". The tests compare
against `std.sort.block`, an independent implementation of a different
algorithm, as a model: `test_sort.zig` sweeps (element sizes × lengths at
every cut × nine input patterns) and the `SORT_FUZZ` driver. The comparison
counts quoted above were taken once by a disposable probe (Rust's closure
counting next to ours). They are a check of the port's fidelity, not an
anchor.

## What is deliberately not done

- Rust's `optimize_for_size` variants (heapsort-only unstable, plain merge
  sort stable). Not now: no consumer asks for size, and the zig-libs
  build-option mechanism (CONVENTIONS §4.2) is where it would go.
- Panicking on a detected order violation, as Rust does. Never: see
  "Algorithm", point 1.

## Backlog / deferred

- **Backlog: radix sort for integer keys** (`u32`/`u64`/`i64`/`f64` via a
  key function). Rust std has none; a measured win over ipnsort on
  ≥ 10⁴ random integer keys would be an `**Ahead:** speed` claim.
- **Backlog: candidate consumers** (surveyed 2026-10-25, sort share not yet
  profiled): zstd dict_builder, tsdb, finstats/metrics/latency-stats
  percentiles (`selectNth`), tabular, netaddr `IpSetBuilder`, geoindex,
  kvtree, kv, trie builder, jinja `sort` filter (stable).
- **Backlog: measure crumsort/fluxsort and vqsort** as further "fastest"
  candidates for integer keys (C, Unlicense / C++, Apache-2.0); the card's
  fastest is over Rust std and C++ libstdc++ only.
- **Backlog: parallel sort** (rayon `par_sort` shape) over `std.Io` tasks.
- **Not doing: `partial_sort`.** `selectNth(k)` then `unstable` on
  `items[0..k]` is the same result.
